Reading route

The numbered sections follow the slides in the same order, and each slide links to its section here. The notebook adds the R output and the explanations for study after class. One series, Australian holiday trips, runs through all seven.

  1. From Holt-Winters to ETS: what Session 18 left us with, and one line of R that fits, chooses and forecasts.
  2. The ETS letters: Error, Trend and Season, and the models you have already fitted.
  3. From a method to a statistical model: the observation equation, additive and multiplicative errors, and one update by hand in both forms.
  4. Fitting by likelihood: how a prediction’s distribution scores an observation, and the score ETS() maximizes.
  5. Choosing by AICc: AIC and AICc by hand, the parameter count, and the scoreboard behind automatic selection.
  6. Check the selected model: the residual checks on the innovation residuals.
  7. Forecasting with ETS: forecast distributions, one interval by hand, whether an interval repeats with its point forecast, and the whole route in one table.

The required work is Exercises 1 and 2, Exercise 3 parts 1, 2 and 4, and its calculator comparison; Exercise 3 part 3 is optional. The appendix holds BIC, the nested-model argument, comparisons across model families, zeros and transformations, simulated intervals, and where the likelihood score comes from.

References

  1. Hyndman, R.J., & Athanasopoulos, G. (2021). Forecasting: principles and practice (3rd ed.), sections 8.4 to 8.7. https://otexts.com/fpp3/
  2. Hyndman, R. J., Koehler, A. B., Ord, J. K., & Snyder, R. D. (2008). Forecasting with exponential smoothing: The state space approach. Springer-Verlag.
  3. Akaike, H. (1974). A new look at the statistical model identification. IEEE Transactions on Automatic Control, 19, 716-723.

Libraries

library(fpp3)

Before class: a short likelihood guide

Allow about ten minutes. We keep the observations fixed and ask which model settings make them more plausible.

  1. Prediction and uncertainty belong together. A forecast of 100 with a standard deviation of 2 describes a different distribution from a forecast of 100 with a standard deviation of 20.
  2. Density is not a probability at a point. For continuous data, likelihood uses the heights of probability density curves at the observations. These heights need not be below one.
  3. A time series uses conditional densities. At each date, predict using earlier information; evaluate that observation under its conditional distribution. Multiply those densities to obtain the likelihood, or add their logarithms to obtain the log-likelihood.
  4. Fit and complexity are separate questions. Fitting chooses a model’s parameters. Model selection also asks whether extra flexibility earns its place.
  5. Forecast evaluation asks a different question. AICc, defined below, is a fit score with a penalty for extra parameters. Like the SSE in Session 16 on fitting SES, it is computed on the training data, whereas rolling-origin evaluation, as in Session 14 on cross-validation, measures actual forecast errors at specified horizons.

Check your understanding: What stays fixed during estimation? Why is a very wide distribution not automatically a good fit? What is the difference between estimating alpha and selecting the trend type? Which errors matter for a twelve-month inventory decision? Why must model selection be repeated inside each training fold when evaluating an automatic procedure?

TipAnswers: open after trying the questions
  • What stays fixed during estimation? The observations. Fitting varies the parameters and initial states and asks which values make those fixed data most plausible.
  • Why is a very wide distribution not automatically a good fit? Widening a distribution lowers its curve near the center, where well-predicted observations fall, and a very wide one is low everywhere. The heights at the observations shrink, so the likelihood falls.
  • Estimating alpha or selecting the trend type? Estimating alpha is fitting: the form is fixed, and the likelihood chooses the value. Selecting the trend type compares different forms, each fitted first, so it needs a criterion that charges for the extra parameters, such as AICc.
  • Which errors matter for a twelve-month inventory decision? Forecast errors at horizons up to twelve months, on data the model did not use for fitting. One-step training residuals do not measure them.
  • Why repeat selection inside each training fold? Automatic selection is part of the procedure being evaluated. Choosing the form once on the full series would let earlier folds use information from their future.

The handwritten 19_A_MLE_Informal_Intro.pdf is optional background. No calculus proof or memorization of the general likelihood derivation is needed for this session.

1. From Holt-Winters to ETS

Last session. In Session 18 on Holt-Winters we chose the seasonal form ourselves. The time plot suggested a seasonal effect, we wrote season("A") or season("M") into ETS(), and ETS() estimated the weights and initial states of the form we wrote. Held-out quarters then judged the choice.

Today. We let ETS() choose the form as well. With no letters in the formula, it fits every eligible combination of error, trend and season, ranks them with a score called AICc, and keeps the best. Its forecast comes with a distribution for every future quarter, which gives the intervals. We then check the chosen model and read its forecasts.

Session 18: Holt-Winters Today: ETS
The form we chose it from the time plot and wrote it into ETS() ETS() tries every eligible form
Fitting ETS() estimated the weights and initial states the same fitting, now explained: maximum likelihood
Choosing held-out errors on later quarters AICc on the training data, then residual checks; held-out errors still settle close calls
The forecast a path a path with a distribution, and so an interval, at every horizon

Quarterly Australian holiday trips, in millions, as in Session 18. The first model is Session 18’s additive Holt-Winters; the second writes no letters, so ETS() chooses:

aus_holidays <- tourism |>
  filter(Purpose == "Holiday") |>
  summarise(Trips = sum(Trips) / 1e3)

fit_open <- aus_holidays |>
  model(
    additive = ETS(Trips ~ error("A") + trend("A") + season("A")),
    auto     = ETS(Trips)
  )

fit_open
# A mable: 1 x 2
      additive         auto
       <model>      <model>
1 <ETS(A,A,A)> <ETS(M,N,A)>
fit_open |>
  forecast(h = 8) |>
  autoplot(aus_holidays, level = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Session 18's model against the automatic choice",
       y = "Overnight trips (millions)")

The mable shows the automatic choice, \(ETS(M,N,A)\). Its forecasts repeat the seasons on a flat path: 12.7 million trips for 2018 Q1 and again for 2019 Q1, where additive Holt-Winters rises from 12.9 to 13.4 million. In this run ETS() chose \(ETS(M,N,A)\); a future software version could choose differently, so read the model name in the output. Sections 2 and 3 read its three letters, and section 5 shows why the score preferred a model with no trend.

We keep the automatic model as fit for the rest of the notebook:

fit <- fit_open |> select(auto)

2. The ETS letters

ETS stands for Error, Trend and Season, the three letters of every model name, in that order:

  • Error: A additive or M multiplicative.
  • Trend: N none, A additive or Ad additive damped. Multiplicative trends are outside this course.
  • Season: N none, A additive or M multiplicative.

The trend and season letters set the method: the recursions of Sessions 15 to 18. The error letter turns the method into a statistical model, the subject of section 3. You have fitted these models before:

Model Method Where you met it
\(ETS(A,N,N)\) simple exponential smoothing Sessions 15 and 16
\(ETS(A,A,N)\) Holt’s linear trend Session 17
\(ETS(A,A,A)\) additive Holt-Winters Session 18
\(ETS(M,A,M)\) multiplicative Holt-Winters Session 18

Three of them on the same holiday trips show what the trend and season letters do to a forecast:

fit_letters <- aus_holidays |>
  model(
    `ETS(A,N,N)` = ETS(Trips ~ error("A") + trend("N") + season("N")),
    `ETS(A,A,N)` = ETS(Trips ~ error("A") + trend("A") + season("N")),
    `ETS(A,A,A)` = ETS(Trips ~ error("A") + trend("A") + season("A"))
  )
fit_letters |>
  forecast(h = 8) |>
  autoplot(aus_holidays |> filter(year(Quarter) >= 2010), level = NULL) +
  labs(title = "N, N is flat; a trend adds a slope; a season adds the quarters",
       y = "Overnight trips (millions)", colour = "Model")

With no trend and no season the forecast is flat at the last level. An additive trend adds a slope. An additive season puts the quarters back. The error letter does not show in these point forecasts; section 3 shows what it changes. Notebook 19_A collects the nine trend and season combinations and the fpp3 table of their recursions, as reference.

Check: name a model. You want errors measured in the data’s units, a slope that keeps shrinking the further ahead you forecast, and no seasonal pattern. Which ETS model is it? Then read the automatic choice of section 1, \(ETS(M,N,A)\), one letter at a time. Commit before opening.

TipAnswer: open after naming the model
  • Errors in the data’s units: A. A slope that keeps shrinking: Ad, the damped trend. No seasonal pattern: N. The model is \(ETS(A,Ad,N)\), damped Holt from Session 17.
  • \(ETS(M,N,A)\): M, misses are proportions of the prediction, so they grow with the level; N, the forecasts carry no slope; A, each quarter adds a fixed number of trips to the level. 19_A ends with the same reading as a check.

3. From a method to a statistical model

Write simple exponential smoothing (SES) in the order of Sessions 17 and 18: predict \(y_t\), then update the level. The prediction \(\hat y_{t|t-1}\) is called the prior prediction because it is made before \(y_t\) is observed, from the level \(\ell_{t-1}\) available at that time. The colored line is new:

\[ \begin{align*} &\text{Predict } y_t && \hat y_{t|t-1}=\ell_{t-1}\\ &\text{Update the level} && \ell_t=\ell_{t-1}+\alpha e_t,\qquad e_t=y_t-\hat y_{t|t-1}\\ &\textcolor{#B5471E}{\text{Observation}} && \textcolor{#B5471E}{y_t=\ell_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t,\qquad \varepsilon_t\sim N(0,\sigma^2)\text{, independent over time}} \end{align*} \]

The first two lines are the SES method in its error-correction form from Session 15 on SES equations. The new line says which values \(y_t\) could take before it is observed: the prior prediction plus a random surprise \(\varepsilon_t\), the innovation, normal with mean zero and variance \(\sigma^2\). With it, the method becomes a statistical model, \(ETS(A,N,N)\), and three things follow:

  • A prediction is the center of a distribution. Before \(y_t\) arrives, the model says \(y_t\sim N(\ell_{t-1},\sigma^2)\). Section 4 scores each observation against that distribution.
  • One surprise moves both. The same innovation that moves \(y_t\) away from its prediction moves the level, by \(\alpha\) times its size. This is why fpp3 calls these models innovations state space models (fpp3 8.5).
  • Future surprises are unknown. Each one will move a future level, so the model gives a distribution of possible paths, and with it forecast intervals.

After fitting, \(e_t=y_t-\hat y_{t|t-1}\), computed at the estimated settings, is the fitted innovation residual: an estimate of the surprise that actually happened. fable calls the prior prediction the fitted value, .fitted.

Multiplicative errors

With multiplicative errors the surprise is a proportion of the prediction. The colored terms change:

\[ \begin{align*} &\text{Predict } y_t && \hat y_{t|t-1}=\ell_{t-1}\\ &\text{Error} && \textcolor{#B5471E}{\varepsilon_t=\frac{y_t-\hat y_{t|t-1}}{\hat y_{t|t-1}}}\\ &\text{Update the level} && \ell_t=\ell_{t-1}\textcolor{#B5471E}{(1+\alpha\varepsilon_t)}\\ &\text{Observation} && y_t=\ell_{t-1}\textcolor{#B5471E}{(1+\varepsilon_t)},\qquad \varepsilon_t\sim N(0,\sigma^2) \end{align*} \]

This is \(ETS(M,N,N)\). An innovation of \(0.05\) is an observation 5% above its prediction. Multiply out the level update: \(\ell_{t-1}+\alpha\ell_{t-1}\varepsilon_t=\ell_{t-1}+\alpha(y_t-\hat y_{t|t-1})\), the additive update again. With the parameters and states held fixed, the error letter does not change the point recursion; the hand calculation below checks it. What it changes is the size of surprise the model expects: \(\sigma\) is now a proportion, so a miss of a given number of trips is more likely when the level is high. That changes the likelihood, so models fitted separately with A and M errors can have different estimates, point forecasts and intervals.

Multiplicative errors need strictly positive data. ETS() does not consider them for a series with zeros or negative values; the appendix explains why a transformation does not simply fix that.

What the error letter changes in R

Fit the automatic choice and its additive-error twin, then compare the widths of their 95% intervals, quarter by quarter:

fit_errors <- aus_holidays |>
  model(
    additive       = ETS(Trips ~ error("A") + trend("N") + season("A")),
    multiplicative = ETS(Trips ~ error("M") + trend("N") + season("A"))
  )

widths <- fit_errors |>
  forecast(h = 8) |>
  hilo(level = 95) |>
  unpack_hilo(`95%`) |>
  mutate(width = `95%_upper` - `95%_lower`)

widths |>
  as_tibble() |>
  select(.model, Quarter, .mean, width)
# A tibble: 16 × 4
   .model         Quarter .mean width
   <chr>            <qtr> <dbl> <dbl>
 1 additive       2018 Q1  12.7  1.74
 2 additive       2018 Q2  10.9  1.85
 3 additive       2018 Q3  10.5  1.96
 4 additive       2018 Q4  10.7  2.06
 5 additive       2019 Q1  12.7  2.15
 6 additive       2019 Q2  10.9  2.25
 7 additive       2019 Q3  10.5  2.33
 8 additive       2019 Q4  10.7  2.42
 9 multiplicative 2018 Q1  12.7  2.31
10 multiplicative 2018 Q2  10.9  2.14
11 multiplicative 2018 Q3  10.5  2.18
12 multiplicative 2018 Q4  10.6  2.31
13 multiplicative 2019 Q1  12.7  2.71

16 multiplicative 2019 Q4  10.6  2.71
widths |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Quarter, y = width, colour = .model)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  labs(title = "Additive errors widen steadily; multiplicative errors follow the season",
       y = "Width of the 95% interval (millions of trips)", colour = "Errors")

The point forecasts of the two models agree to within 0.1 million trips. The intervals do not:

  • Additive errors: the width grows steadily with the horizon, from 1.74 million trips in 2018 Q1 to 2.42 in 2019 Q4. A surprise has the same spread in trips whatever the quarter.
  • Multiplicative errors: the width follows the season. It is largest in Q1, the peak, and falls from 2018 Q1 to 2018 Q2 although the horizon grows, because Q2 forecasts fewer trips and a proportional surprise is then smaller in trips. Compare the same quarter a year later and it grows: 2.31 in 2018 Q1, 2.71 in 2019 Q1.

Response and innovation residuals

The random innovation belongs to the model; an innovation residual is reconstructed after fitting. With multiplicative errors, response and innovation residuals differ. augment() returns both:

  • Response residuals (.resid): \(y_t - \hat{y}_{t|t-1}\), in the data’s units.
  • Innovation residuals (.innov):
    • additive error model: \(\hat{\varepsilon}_t = y_t - \hat{y}_{t|t-1}\);
    • multiplicative error model: \(\hat{\varepsilon}_t = \dfrac{y_t - \hat{y}_{t|t-1}}{\hat{y}_{t|t-1}}\), a relative error.

For multiplicative errors, apply the checks from Session 9 on residual diagnostics to .innov, because this is the relative error the model assumes. The holiday-trips model has multiplicative errors, so its diagnostics use .innov.

One update by hand, in both error forms

Take made-up numbers. Two models with no trend and no season, \(ETS(A,N,N)\) and \(ETS(M,N,N)\), both have the level \(\ell_{t-1}=100\) and \(\alpha=0.3\). The observation is \(y_t=106\). For each model: predict \(y_t\), compute the error, update the level and predict \(y_{t+1}\). Then say what .resid and .innov would show for this quarter. Commit to your numbers before opening.

TipWorked example: open after trying it
Step \(ETS(A,N,N)\) \(ETS(M,N,N)\)
Predict \(y_t\) \(\textcolor{#1F3A4D}{\hat y_{t\mid t-1}}=\textcolor{#1F3A4D}{\ell_{t-1}}=\textcolor{#1F3A4D}{100}\) \(\textcolor{#1F3A4D}{\hat y_{t\mid t-1}}=\textcolor{#1F3A4D}{\ell_{t-1}}=\textcolor{#1F3A4D}{100}\)
Error \(e_t=106-\textcolor{#1F3A4D}{100}=6\) \(\varepsilon_t=(106-\textcolor{#1F3A4D}{100})/\textcolor{#1F3A4D}{100}=0.06\)
Update the level \(\textcolor{#B5471E}{\ell_t}=\textcolor{#1F3A4D}{100}+0.3\times6=\textcolor{#B5471E}{101.8}\) \(\textcolor{#B5471E}{\ell_t}=\textcolor{#1F3A4D}{100}(1+0.3\times0.06)=\textcolor{#B5471E}{101.8}\)
Predict \(y_{t+1}\) \(\textcolor{#B5471E}{\hat y_{t+1\mid t}}=\textcolor{#B5471E}{101.8}\) \(\textcolor{#B5471E}{\hat y_{t+1\mid t}}=\textcolor{#B5471E}{101.8}\)
.resid and .innov 6 and 6 6 and 0.06

Slate marks what was known before the observation, the observation 106 is in black, and orange marks the updated level and its prediction, as in Sessions 17 and 18.

With the same \(\alpha\) and the same level, the two models update to the same level and make the same next prediction. They differ in what they expect of the next surprise. Additive errors expect the same spread in units at any level; multiplicative errors expect the same spread as a proportion, so their spread in units grows with the level. That is the pattern of interval widths above, and it is why the two models score the same data differently when they are fitted.

4. Fitting by likelihood

Score each prediction’s distribution at its observation

In Session 16 on fitting SES, we fitted by searching: each candidate pair of \(\alpha\) and \(\ell_0\) received a score, its SSE, and the search kept the best. Since Session 17, ETS() has done the fitting, and its score is the likelihood:

  1. For each training quarter, take the distribution of the prior prediction, from section 3.
  2. Read the height of its density curve at the observed \(y_t\).
  3. Multiply the heights over all training quarters to get the likelihood, or add their logarithms to get the log-likelihood.

A higher likelihood means the observations are more plausible under that candidate’s predictions. For continuous data, a density height is not the probability of one exact value, and it can be larger than one. The short likelihood guide explains the distinction.

One quarter of the selected model shows step 2. Its distribution is normal, centered on the prior prediction, with a standard deviation of the prediction times \(\sigma\), because the errors are relative:

sigma2 <- glance(fit)$sigma2

one_quarter <- augment(fit) |>
  filter(Quarter == yearquarter("2017 Q1")) |>
  mutate(sd = .fitted * sqrt(sigma2),
         height = dnorm(Trips, mean = .fitted, sd = sd),
         height_wide = dnorm(Trips, mean = .fitted, sd = 3 * sd))

one_quarter |>
  as_tibble() |>
  select(Quarter, Trips, .fitted, sd, height, height_wide)
# A tibble: 1 × 6
  Quarter Trips .fitted    sd height height_wide
    <qtr> <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>       <dbl>
1 2017 Q1  12.4    12.1 0.560  0.592       0.233
tibble(y = seq(10, 14.2, by = 0.01)) |>
  mutate(fitted = dnorm(y, one_quarter$.fitted, one_quarter$sd),
         `three times wider` = dnorm(y, one_quarter$.fitted, 3 * one_quarter$sd)) |>
  pivot_longer(-y, names_to = "distribution", values_to = "density") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = y, y = density, colour = distribution)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = one_quarter$Trips) +
  labs(title = "2017 Q1: the score is the curve's height at the observation",
       x = "Overnight trips (millions)", y = "Density")

Check: why is a very wide distribution not automatically a good fit? It cannot miss badly, so it may seem safe. Commit before opening.

TipAnswer: open after deciding

Widening a distribution lowers its curve near the center, where well-predicted observations fall. For 2017 Q1 the fitted curve is 0.59 high at the observation; a curve three times wider is only 0.23 high there, so the score falls. A badly predicted quarter, such as 2017 Q4, gains a little from a wider curve. The likelihood adds up all 80 quarters, so the width that scores best balances the two: that is how fitting estimates \(\sigma\).

The same search as Session 16, with a new score

ETS() searches for the values of \(\alpha\), \(\gamma\) and the initial states that give the highest log-likelihood. To see the score’s shape, take a slice through the search: hold \(\gamma\), the initial level and the initial seasonal states at their fitted values, vary \(\alpha\) alone, and for each candidate run the predict-observe-update loop through the 80 quarters, as in Session 16. For \(ETS(M,N,A)\) the updates are those of additive seasonal smoothing without a slope, written in error-correction form:

est <- fit |> tidy() |> select(term, estimate) |> deframe()

loglik_mna <- function(alpha, y = aus_holidays$Trips) {
  level  <- est[["l[0]"]]
  season <- est[c("s[-3]", "s[-2]", "s[-1]", "s[0]")]  # Q1 to Q4 before 1998 Q1
  pred <- err <- numeric(length(y))
  for (t in seq_along(y)) {
    pred[t] <- level + season[1]                    # predict y_t
    err[t]  <- (y[t] - pred[t]) / pred[t]           # relative error
    level   <- level + alpha * (y[t] - pred[t])     # update the level
    season  <- c(season[-1], season[1] + est[["gamma"]] * (y[t] - pred[t]))  # update the season
  }
  -0.5 * (length(y) * log(sum(err^2)) + 2 * sum(log(pred)))  # fable's log-likelihood
}

c(by_hand = loglik_mna(est[["alpha"]]), glance = glance(fit)$log_lik)
  by_hand    glance 
-106.1145 -106.1145

The function reproduces the log-likelihood glance() reports. The last line is fable’s formula for multiplicative errors: small relative errors raise the score, and the second term converts them back to trips. It leaves out constants that are the same for every candidate; the appendix shows where it comes from. Now vary \(\alpha\):

slice <- tibble(alpha = seq(0.1, 0.7, by = 0.01)) |>
  mutate(log_lik = sapply(alpha, loglik_mna))

slice |>
  ggplot(aes(x = alpha, y = log_lik)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = est[["alpha"]], linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(title = "The slice peaks at the fitted alpha",
       x = "alpha (gamma and initial states at their fitted values)",
       y = "Log-likelihood")

The slice peaks at the fitted \(\alpha\approx0.35\). A small \(\alpha\) lets the level lag the rise since 2015; a large one chases each quarter’s surprise. ETS() searched over six values at once: \(\alpha\), \(\gamma\), the initial level and the three free initial seasonal states. The slice shows one direction through that search near its end point. The innovation variance \(\sigma^2\) is not part of the search: for any candidate, its best value follows from that candidate’s errors, as the appendix shows. The AIC still counts it, as the seventh estimated value of section 5.

  • Additive errors. With normal errors, the candidate with the highest likelihood is the one with the smallest SSE. The additive-error fits of Sessions 16 to 18 are therefore the same whichever score you think of.
  • Multiplicative errors. The two scores differ: the likelihood scores relative errors and includes the conversion term. ETS() maximizes the likelihood in both cases.

5. Choosing by AICc

AIC: fit plus a charge for every estimated value

The likelihood chooses values within a form. To compare different forms, we need a score that also charges for flexibility, because a form with more parameters can usually fit the training data a little better. Akaike’s Information Criterion adds that charge, in color:

\[ \text{AIC} = -2\log(L)\textcolor{#B5471E}{{}+2k} \]

  • \(L\) is the maximized likelihood of the model.
  • \(k\) is the number of values that have been estimated: parameters and free initial states, including the residual variance. It measures the complexity of the model.

Among comparable candidates, prefer the smaller AIC. Improving fit lowers the first term, while every extra estimated value adds 2. Here \(k\) includes the variance, unlike the \(K\) in the residual-scale correction of Session 16 on fitting SES.

AICc: the bias-corrected AIC

For small samples (small \(T\), the length of the series), the AIC tends to choose models with too many parameters. The corrected version charges more:

\[ \text{AIC}_{\text{c}} = \text{AIC}\textcolor{#B5471E}{{}+\frac{2k(k+1)}{T-k-1}} \]

As with the AIC, lower is better. ETS() uses the \(AIC_c\) by default when it chooses a model.

Reading the selected model

The continuing example is aus_holidays, built in section 1: holiday trips summed over regions and converted from thousands to millions. fit is its automatic model.

Four functions read a fitted model. report() shows which form was chosen, together with its estimates and criteria. tidy() returns the estimates as a table, one estimate per row. glance() returns a single summary row for each model, with log_lik, AIC, AICc and BIC among its columns. components() returns the paths of the level and the seasonal states, which autoplot() draws.

1 auto     -106.  226.  228.  243.
fit |> components() |> autoplot()
Warning: Removed 11 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
(`geom_line()`).

Read the three letters before interpreting the parameters:

  • M, multiplicative errors. Misses scale with the level. report() rounds \(\sigma^2\) to 0.0022 (0.00215 before rounding), so a one-step relative miss has a standard deviation of about \(\sqrt{0.00215}\approx0.046\), or 4.6% of the prediction.
  • N, no trend. The forecasts carry no slope.
  • A, additive seasonality. Each quarter’s effect is a fixed number of trips. The initial seasonal states put Q1 about 1.52 million trips above the level and Q3 about 0.69 million below it. As in Session 18 on Holt-Winters, tidy() lists them backward in time: s[-3] is Q1 and s[0] is Q4.
  • The weights. \(\alpha\approx0.35\) lets the level adapt, while \(\gamma\approx0.0001\) means that the seasonal pattern barely changes over the twenty years.

Counting \(k\). glance() computes the AIC with \(k=7\) for this model. tidy() lists seven estimates, but the four initial seasonal states are constrained to sum to zero (\(1.519-0.293-0.688-0.538\approx0\)), so only three of them are free. Add \(\alpha\), \(\gamma\), \(\ell_0\) and the innovation variance \(\sigma^2\), and \(k=3+4=7\). Then AIC \(=-2(-106.114)+2\times7=226.23\), as glance() reports. The calculator comparison supplies \(k\) for its models.

Check: does a trend earn its place? Session 18 on Holt-Winters fitted holiday trips with an additive trend. Adding that trend to the selected model gives \(ETS(M,A,A)\), and its log-likelihood rises from \(-106.114\) to \(-104.265\). The trend costs two more estimates, the slope weight \(\beta\) and the initial slope \(b_0\), so \(k=9\). Compute both AIC values: which model does the referee keep? Commit before opening.

TipAnswer: open after choosing a model

\(ETS(M,N,A)\): \(212.23+14=226.23\). \(ETS(M,A,A)\): \(208.53+18=226.53\). The trend raises the log-likelihood by 1.85, so the fit term falls by 3.70, but the penalty rises by 4. The AIC therefore keeps the model without a trend, narrowly. With 80 quarters, the AICc charges more for each extra parameter and widens the gap, 227.78 against 229.10:

fit_trend <- aus_holidays |>
  model(
    MNA = ETS(Trips ~ error("M") + trend("N") + season("A")),
    MAA = ETS(Trips ~ error("M") + trend("A") + season("A"))
  )

fit_trend |>
  glance() |>
  select(.model, log_lik, AIC, AICc) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)
.model log_lik AIC AICc
MNA -106.11 226.23 227.78
MAA -104.26 226.53 229.10

knitr::kable(digits = 2) prints the table with two decimals, whereas a tibble would print these values as whole numbers, such as 226.. The referee keeps \(ETS(M,N,A)\), the model the automatic search chose.

Automatic ETS model selection

How to ask ETS() to choose

When the formula does not fix a component, ETS() tries every allowed option for it and keeps the model with the lowest \(AIC_c\). With no specials, ETS(y) searches applicable combinations. Frequency, positivity, data length and fitting restrictions can reduce the candidates; annual nonseasonal data do not get seasonal models.

Model combinations that are excluded

The search is also smaller than the list of letters suggests. Three combinations of (Error, Trend, Season) can be numerically unstable, because their state equations divide by values that may be close to zero:

  • \(ETS(A, N, M)\)
  • \(ETS(A, A, M)\)
  • \(ETS(A, Ad, M)\)

They are not considered when ETS() chooses a model. With trends N, A and Ad, errors A and M, and seasons N, A and M, that leaves 15 of the 18 combinations.

The scoreboard behind the choice

Fitting the 15 eligible models ourselves shows what ETS(Trips) compared:

fit_all <- aus_holidays |>
  model(
    ANN  = ETS(Trips ~ error("A") + trend("N")  + season("N")),
    AAN  = ETS(Trips ~ error("A") + trend("A")  + season("N")),
    AAdN = ETS(Trips ~ error("A") + trend("Ad") + season("N")),
    ANA  = ETS(Trips ~ error("A") + trend("N")  + season("A")),
    AAA  = ETS(Trips ~ error("A") + trend("A")  + season("A")),
    AAdA = ETS(Trips ~ error("A") + trend("Ad") + season("A")),
    MNN  = ETS(Trips ~ error("M") + trend("N")  + season("N")),
    MAN  = ETS(Trips ~ error("M") + trend("A")  + season("N")),
    MAdN = ETS(Trips ~ error("M") + trend("Ad") + season("N")),
    MNA  = ETS(Trips ~ error("M") + trend("N")  + season("A")),
    MAA  = ETS(Trips ~ error("M") + trend("A")  + season("A")),
    MAdA = ETS(Trips ~ error("M") + trend("Ad") + season("A")),
    MNM  = ETS(Trips ~ error("M") + trend("N")  + season("M")),
    MAM  = ETS(Trips ~ error("M") + trend("A")  + season("M")),
    MAdM = ETS(Trips ~ error("M") + trend("Ad") + season("M"))
  )

scores <- fit_all |>
  glance() |>
  select(.model, AICc) |>
  mutate(gap = AICc - min(AICc)) |>
  arrange(AICc)

scores |> knitr::kable(digits = 2)
.model AICc gap
MNA 227.78 0.00
MNM 228.34 0.56
MAA 229.10 1.32
MAM 229.29 1.51
ANA 230.05 2.27
AAA 231.14 3.35
MAdM 231.33 3.55
MAdA 232.10 4.31
AAdA 232.37 4.59
AAN 364.74 136.95
MAN 365.77 137.99
AAdN 367.63 139.84
ANN 367.64 139.86
MAdN 368.42 140.64
MNN 368.59 140.80 
scores |>
  ggplot(aes(x = gap, y = reorder(.model, -gap))) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(title = "Seasonality decides; the top three are close",
       x = "AICc minus the lowest AICc", y = NULL)

The scoreboard answers two questions at two scales. Every seasonal model beats every nonseasonal one by more than 130: seasonality is not in doubt. At the top, \(ETS(M,N,M)\) is 0.56 behind and \(ETS(M,A,A)\) 1.32 behind. A gap that small says the data hardly separate the three; the AICc still has to name one, and it names \(ETS(M,N,A)\).

When AICc can compare models

Use AICc between models fitted to the same observations on the same response scale, as all 15 above are. The A-error and M-error models can be compared because both likelihoods are densities of the same \(y\), although their residuals are on different scales. Do not compare the reported AICc of a model for y with one for log(y): the likelihoods are of different variables.

When that comparability is in doubt, or when the decision depends on a particular horizon, compare forecasts on held-out data instead, with rolling-origin evaluation from Session 14 on cross-validation. That is also the way to separate close candidates such as the top three above. The appendix gives the general condition.

6. Check the selected model

In-class check. Work through the four residual checks of Session 9 on residual diagnostics, using the innovation residuals. Where does the selected model still fall short? Discuss before opening the interpretation.

fit |> gg_tsresiduals()
augment(fit) |> features(.innov, ljung_box, lag = 8)
# A tibble: 1 × 3
  .model lb_stat lb_pvalue
  <chr>    <dbl>     <dbl>
1 auto      6.57     0.584

All three panels plot the innovation residuals, .innov, although the histogram’s axis is labeled .resid.

TipWorked interpretation: open after discussing in class
  • Mean (time plot). The innovations average about +0.5%, so on average the prior predictions were slightly too low.
  • Spread (time plot). From 1998 to 2004 the misses stay within about ±6%; from 2005 on they reach about ±10%. The spread is not constant, which matters for the width of the intervals.
  • Autocorrelation (ACF and Ljung–Box). Only the bar at lag 14 crosses the band, and the Ljung–Box test with lag 8, twice the quarterly period, gives p = 0.58. There is little evidence of autocorrelation at short lags.
  • Distribution shape (histogram). Roughly symmetric around zero. As in Session 12 on prediction intervals, normality matters for the intervals, not for the point forecasts.
  • What the model still misses. 11 of the last 12 innovations are positive. The series rises from 2015, and a model without a trend keeps predicting too little, so its forecasts start from slightly behind.

Inspect innovation residuals for remaining structure. If the chosen model leaves predictable patterns, reconsider the candidates. A low AICc and a nonsignificant test alone do not guarantee suitability for every business horizon.

7. Forecasting with ETS

Generate forecasts only after stating the purpose and horizon. Here eight quarters illustrate the possible path and its uncertainty, in the original units (fpp3 8.7). First the point forecasts alone; the intervals follow the check below.

fc <- fit |> forecast(h = 8)

fc |>
  autoplot(aus_holidays, level = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Australian domestic tourism: point forecasts",
       y = "Overnight trips (millions)")

For this \(ETS(M,N,A)\) model, forecast() returns a normal distribution for each quarter, with no simulation. Its mean, in the .mean column, is the point forecast, and its 95% interval is the mean plus or minus 1.96 forecast standard deviations. With multiplicative errors, the spread is proportional to the level of the series. Other ETS models may simulate their intervals; the appendix explains how.

The one-step interval by hand

The first forecast, 2018 Q1, is one step ahead, so its distribution is the one from section 4: normal, centered on the point forecast, with a standard deviation of the point forecast times \(\sigma\). Print the mean and standard deviation with four decimals:

fc |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(mean = mean(Trips), sd = sqrt(distributional::variance(Trips))) |>
  select(Quarter, mean, sd) |>
  head(1) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 4)
Quarter mean sd
2018 Q1 12.6954 0.5891

With \(\sigma=\sqrt{0.002153}=0.0464\), the standard deviation is \(12.695\times0.0464=0.589\), and the 95% interval is \(12.695\pm1.96\times0.589\), that is \([11.54,\,13.85]\) million trips, as hilo() reports below. Rounding the mean to 12.7 before multiplying moves the lower end to 11.55: carry the decimals until the last step.

Will the interval repeat too?

Check. The point forecast for 2019 Q1 equals the one for 2018 Q1, 12.70 million trips, because the model has no trend and its seasonal pattern is fixed. Will the two 95% intervals match as well? Commit before opening.

TipAnswer: open after predicting

No. The 2018 Q1 interval is [11.54, 13.85], and the 2019 Q1 interval widens to [11.34, 14.05]. The point forecast repeats, but four more quarters of possible surprises can move the level, so the uncertainty grows with the horizon even when the point forecasts repeat.

fc |>
  hilo(level = 95) |>
  as_tibble() |>
  select(Quarter, .mean, `95%`)
# A tibble: 8 × 3
  Quarter .mean                   `95%`
    <qtr> <dbl>                  <hilo>

2 2018 Q2  10.9 [ 9.814061, 11.95109]95
3 2018 Q3  10.5 [ 9.396164, 11.57892]95
4 2018 Q4  10.6 [ 9.485864, 11.79090]95
5 2019 Q1  12.7 [11.339233, 14.05161]95

The fan chart draws the 80% and 95% intervals for every quarter:

fc |>
  autoplot(aus_holidays) +
  labs(title = "Australian domestic tourism: forecast intervals",
       y = "Overnight trips (millions)")

Compare quarters a year apart, not neighbors. As in section 3, a multiplicative-error interval can be narrower in Q2 than in the Q1 before it, because Q2 forecasts fewer trips; the same quarter a year later is always wider.

The route for holiday trips

Step Tool What it gave for holiday trips
Choose a form the three ETS letters 15 eligible forms; \(ETS(M,N,A)\) reads as proportional misses, no slope, fixed seasonal effects in trips
Fit maximum likelihood \(\alpha\approx0.35\), \(\gamma\approx0.0001\), the initial level and seasonal states, and \(\sigma^2\approx0.0022\)
Select AICc \(ETS(M,N,A)\), with \(ETS(M,N,M)\) and \(ETS(M,A,A)\) close behind
Check innovation residuals little autocorrelation, but 11 of the last 12 misses positive since the rise of 2015
Forecast forecast distributions flat seasonal path at 12.7 million for each Q1, intervals that widen with the horizon

Suppose the decision is next summer’s capacity. The AICc barely separates the three leading candidates, and the residuals say the selected model lags a rising series. Held-out evidence settles that kind of close call: compare the candidates’ forecast errors at the horizon of the decision, with rolling-origin evaluation, before committing to one.

  2. Do the response residuals and the innovation residuals match? Check with all.equal() and explain why in one sentence.

A note on units. In millions, the continuing example chose \(ETS(M,N,A)\), with \(ETS(M,N,M)\) close behind: their AICc values are about 0.6 apart. Changing the units multiplies every observation by the same number, which adds the same constant to the log-likelihood of every model, so in theory the ranking cannot change. In practice the numerical search can flip such a near-tie. As with optim() in Session 16 on fitting SES, the search only tells us where it stopped, and an AICc gap of 0.6 is still too small to mean anything. To choose between two such close models, compare their forecasts on a test set or by cross-validation.

  filter(Purpose == "Holiday") |>

Calculator comparison

For the fixed ETS(A,A,A) model in Exercise 3, take log_lik from glance(), rounded to two decimals, and calculate AIC using \(k=17\). For a second fixed candidate ETS(M,Ad,M) on the same data, use \(k=18\). Compare both AIC values and check them against glance(). How much improvement in log-likelihood is needed to offset one extra parameter? Explain why the lower AIC need not win at your chosen forecast horizon.

A tibble prints a log_lik this large as a whole number, -2776., which is not precise enough here. To read it to two decimals, pipe the selected glance() columns into knitr::kable(digits = 2), as in the continuing example.

The supplied counts include smoothing parameters, free initial states and the innovation variance, counted as in the continuing example: with monthly data, eleven of the twelve initial seasonal states are free. Focus on the fit-versus-complexity tradeoff.

Appendix: supporting explanations

Supporting reading for study after class. None of it is needed for the homework, the group assignments or the final.

Where the likelihood score comes from

For \(ETS(M,N,A)\) the observation equation is \(y_t=\hat y_{t|t-1}(1+\varepsilon_t)\) with \(\varepsilon_t\sim N(0,\sigma^2)\). Given the past, \(y_t\) is normal with mean \(\hat y_{t|t-1}\) and standard deviation \(\hat y_{t|t-1}\sigma\), so its density at the observation is the density of \(\varepsilon_t\) divided by \(\hat y_{t|t-1}\). Adding the logarithms over \(T\) quarters:

\[ \log L=-\frac{T}{2}\log(2\pi\sigma^2)-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_t\varepsilon_t^2-\sum_t\log\hat y_{t|t-1}. \]

For fixed predictions, the best \(\sigma^2\) is \(\sum_t\varepsilon_t^2/T\). Putting it back gives

\[ \log L=-\frac{1}{2}\Big(T\log\sum_t\varepsilon_t^2+2\sum_t\log\hat y_{t|t-1}\Big)+\text{a constant that depends only on }T, \]

which is the last line of loglik_mna() without the constant. fable reports the same quantity. The constant is identical for every model fitted to the same \(T\) observations, so it cannot change a comparison.

For additive errors the term \(\sum_t\log\hat y_{t|t-1}\) is absent and \(\varepsilon_t\) is the error in units, so the log-likelihood is \(-\tfrac{T}{2}\log(\text{SSE})\) plus a constant: the largest likelihood is the smallest SSE. report() prints a \(\sigma^2\) that divides by \(T\) minus the number of estimated parameters, so it is slightly larger than \(\sum_t\varepsilon_t^2/T\).

Reference: BIC, the Bayesian Information Criterion

\[ \text{BIC} = \text{AIC} + k[\log(T)-2] \]

For \(T\geq8\), \(\log T>2\), so BIC puts more weight on the parameter penalty than AIC. Use the same comparable candidate set when interpreting that difference.

Information criteria and nested models

Information criteria combine the likelihood with a penalty for the number of parameters. For nested models fitted to the same data, adding parameters cannot reduce the best achievable likelihood: the larger model can reproduce the smaller one. Arbitrary ETS variants need not be nested. A complexity penalty discourages flexibility that improves training fit without enough evidence of predictive value; it does not guarantee good forecasts.

Comparing across model families

Comparing AICc between ETS candidates fitted to the same observations and response scale is a safe workflow, not a theorem that information criteria can only compare one model family. Across families, likelihood conventions, constants and the observations included must also be compatible. Use rolling-origin evaluation on a common outcome scale when that comparability is uncertain, or when a particular horizon and loss matter (Session 14 on cross-validation).

Zeros, transformations and multiplicative errors

Multiplicative errors are numerically unstable when the data contain zeros or negative values, so ETS() does not consider them for a series that is not strictly positive. For such a series, consider an additive-error specification and inspect its suitability. A transformation changes the modeling scale and requires its own justification; it does not automatically make a multiplicative model admissible. In particular, \(\log(1+x)\) still maps zero to zero.

Other ETS models: point forecasts and simulated intervals

  • Point forecasts. forecast() returns distribution means in .mean for all ETS models. For multiplicative seasonal models, the traditional recursion obtained by setting future errors to zero need not equal that mean; use the returned distribution for decisions involving uncertainty.
  • Intervals. The prediction intervals differ between models with additive and multiplicative components: with multiplicative errors they widen with the level of the series.
  • How they are computed. For some ETS models there is no formula for the forecast variance. Then forecast() simulates many future paths and takes percentiles of them, parametric simulation with errors drawn from the assumed distribution. Residual bootstrapping instead samples fitted innovations; it is a different simulation choice.

The handwritten likelihood primer

The handwritten 19_A_MLE_Informal_Intro.pdf develops maximum likelihood informally, with more steps than the short guide. It is optional background.
